skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: pptx
skills.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates, layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.

skills.name: ast-consistency
skills.description: AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged.

skills.name: body-removal
skills.description: Remove function bodies from Rust/Verus source files to produce signature-only views. Used before the view-design phase to prevent implementation anchoring.

skills.name: bug-reporting
skills.description: Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug.

skills.name: caller-analysis
skills.description: Analyze callers of a Rust module to understand usage expectations for Verus verification. Produces a caller-perspective analysis covering all functions with their visibility and call relationships.

skills.name: crate-analysis
skills.description: Principles for verification order in multi-file Rust crates. Verify top-level modules first (top-down), writing dependency specs on demand as verification drills down. The pipeline tool handles ordering automatically.

skills.name: proof-extraction
skills.description: Extract large inline proof blocks from exec code into named lemmas in .proof.rs. Use when polishing verified code to improve readability and proof organization.

skills.name: proof-minimization
skills.description: Remove redundant proof artifacts (assertions, lemmas, hints, dead code) without weakening guarantees. Use when polishing verified code to reduce verbosity.

skills.name: property-analysis
skills.description: How to analyze source code and identify verification properties — the WHAT of verification. Covers module understanding, property discovery across four dimensions (functional correctness, safety, liveness, structural consistency), and quality review. Use this skill when deciding what to verify for a new module, writing property_analysis.md, or updating global_properties.md.

skills.name: proving-guide
skills.description: Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures.

skills.name: review-methodology
skills.description: Review Verus verification code with focus on spec quality and automated checks.

skills.name: spec-completeness
skills.description: Detect specification incompleteness via nondeterminism checking. Given a Verus function spec, automatically determine whether the spec uniquely determines the output for each valid input. If not, use type-guided binary search to construct a concrete witness (input + two valid but different outputs). No LLM needed — pure SMT-based.

skills.name: spec-design
skills.description: How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs.

skills.name: verification-order
skills.description: Determine function-level verification order within a module using the verification plan. Use at the start of proving to know which function to verify first and how to sequence work.

skills.name: verus-constraints
skills.description: Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code.

skills.name: verus-setup
skills.description: Set up Verus formal verification infrastructure for a Rust project. Covers workspace-level config (vstd dependency, cfg flags, version pinning, Makefile, scripts) and per-crate config (metadata, cfg-gated includes, spec/proof stubs). Use this skill when preparing a repo or crate for Verus verification, adding make verify support, or integrating cheating detection into a build.

skills.name: verus-syntax
skills.description: Verus attribute-based syntax reference for exec functions. Covers #[verus_spec], #[verus_verify], proof!{}, proof_decl!{}, loop invariants. See GUIDE.md for advanced patterns, syntax_attr.rs for the official example.

skills.name: view-design
skills.description: How to design a View type that represents abstract state from the caller's perspective. Input: caller analysis + property concepts. Must NOT see implementation code.

skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings.

---
name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

**Minimal equivalent rewrites** are allowed when Verus genuinely cannot express
a construct. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory. Check `std_specs/`, recent additions.
3. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — rewrite the smallest possible expression
   to an equivalent one Verus accepts. Requirements:
   - Same semantics (identical observable behavior for all inputs)
   - Same panic/error behavior
   - Same asymptotic time and space complexity
   - Smallest possible diff
   - `// VERUS REWRITE: <reason>` comment on the changed code
   - Minimal reproducer proving the original is unsupported
4. **Stdlib wrapper** — if a stdlib/core function call fails because Verus
   cannot handle the parameter types (e.g., `&mut [T]` from `DerefMut`
   coercion, closures), create a thin wrapper function whose body contains
   **ONLY** the stdlib call. Mark the wrapper `external_body` with pre/post
   conditions. The original function calls the wrapper instead. This isolates
   the trust boundary to the thinnest possible layer.

   Example — `core::mem::replace` on `&mut Vec<T>[index]`:
   ```rust
   #[verus_verify(external_body)]
   #[verus_spec(prev =>
       requires index < old(v)@.len(),
       ensures
           prev == old(v)@[index as int],
           v@ == old(v)@.update(index as int, value),
           v@.len() == old(v)@.len(),
   )]
   fn vec_replace<T>(v: &mut Vec<T>, index: usize, value: T) -> T {
       ::core::mem::replace(&mut v[index], value)
   }
   ```
   The wrapper body is a single stdlib call. The `external_body` trusts only
   this one line. The calling function remains fully body-verified.

5. **`external_body` on the original** — absolute last resort. Requires a
   minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry.

**Principle:** prefer rewriting code to a semantic equivalent over ANY cheating.
A rewrite that lets Verus verify the body is always better than `external_body`.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition.
- **Constants**: if the initializer uses only literals and Verus-visible
  symbols, Verus sees it directly — no duplication needed. If it references
  external symbols Verus cannot resolve (e.g. `mem::PAGE_SIZE`), add a
  spec duplicate inside `verus! {}` under `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]` with
  the literal value — but keep the original **ungated** so exec code still
  uses it. Never `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented
in `trust.md`.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in specification phase (must be eliminated in proving) |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's functions**: forbidden — use `admit()` instead. **On dependency functions**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified. See `crate-analysis` skill for the top-down workflow |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |
| `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms. If `uninterp` appears on `View::view()`, that is a consequence of the type being `external_body`, which is already tracked and challenged separately |

## trust.md

`trust.md` records **genuine trust boundaries only** — calls to code
outside the verification scope whose implementation cannot be verified
(hardware registers, inline assembly, MMIO, FFI, std library internals,
external systems). These are the external-bottom boundary.

Items that belong in `trust.md`:
- `assume_specification` for std library / external crate functions
- `external_body` on thin stdlib wrappers that isolate unsupported syntax
- `axiom` for hardware/platform assumptions
- `uninterp spec fn` — banned; if present on `View::view()` of an
  `external_body` type, the trust is tracked under the `external_body` entry

Each entry must include:
1. Function name and file:line location
2. What trust item was used
3. Minimal reproducer proving it cannot be avoided
4. Classification: `STDLIB_WRAPPER` / `EXTERNAL_TYPE` / `HARDWARE_BOUNDARY`

**Do NOT put proof failures in trust.md.** If a function cannot be verified
after exhausting all proof strategies but is not a genuine trust boundary,
record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:

```markdown
## verification-todo.md entry format
- Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
- Status: UNPROVEN
- Attempts: (list strategies tried)
- Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
```

These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

**`axiom` requires human approval** — it introduces arbitrary unverified
axioms with no connection to an external API contract.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
the actual vstd source thoroughly:

```bash
grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
```

Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
`vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## Claiming Verus Limitations

**Principle: isolate and test before concluding.** A failing expression is
evidence only about that expression — not about broader language features —
until a smaller isolated reproducer shows the specific construct also fails.

When `f(|x| expr)` fails, the error might be in `f`, in `|x|`, in `expr`,
or in the combination. You **cannot** conclude "closures are unsupported"
from one failed call. You must test each component separately.

**Do not generalize from an unsupported API to a feature class.** If
`v.sort_by_key(|x| x.field)` fails, that is evidence about `sort_by_key` (or

name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

**Minimal equivalent rewrites** are allowed when Verus genuinely cannot express
a construct. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory. Check `std_specs/`, recent additions.
3. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — rewrite the smallest possible expression
   to an equivalent one Verus accepts. Requirements:
   - Same semantics (identical observable behavior for all inputs)
   - Same panic/error behavior
   - Same asymptotic time and space complexity
   - Smallest possible diff
   - `// VERUS REWRITE: <reason>` comment on the changed code
   - Minimal reproducer proving the original is unsupported
4. **Stdlib wrapper** — if a stdlib/core function call fails because Verus
   cannot handle the parameter types (e.g., `&mut [T]` from `DerefMut`
   coercion, closures), create a thin wrapper function whose body contains
   **ONLY** the stdlib call. Mark the wrapper `external_body` with pre/post
   conditions. The original function calls the wrapper instead. This isolates
   the trust boundary to the thinnest possible layer.

   Example — `core::mem::replace` on `&mut Vec<T>[index]`:
   ```rust
   #[verus_verify(external_body)]
   #[verus_spec(prev =>
       requires index < old(v)@.len(),
       ensures
           prev == old(v)@[index as int],
           v@ == old(v)@.update(index as int, value),
           v@.len() == old(v)@.len(),
   )]
   fn vec_replace<T>(v: &mut Vec<T>, index: usize, value: T) -> T {
       ::core::mem::replace(&mut v[index], value)
   }
   ```
   The wrapper body is a single stdlib call. The `external_body` trusts only
   this one line. The calling function remains fully body-verified.

5. **`external_body` on the original** — absolute last resort. Requires a
   minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry.

A rewrite that lets Verus verify the body is always better than `external_body`.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition.

  spec duplicate inside `verus! {}` under `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]` with

  uses it. Never `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),

source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must

| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |

`trust.md` records **genuine trust boundaries only** — calls to code

- `uninterp spec fn` — banned; if present on `View::view()` of an

4. Classification: `STDLIB_WRAPPER` / `EXTERNAL_TYPE` / `HARDWARE_BOUNDARY`

```markdown
## verification-todo.md entry format
- Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
- Status: UNPROVEN
- Attempts: (list strategies tried)
- Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
```

These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.

whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).

name: proving-guide
description: "Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures."
---

# Proving Guide

Read `verus-constraints` first. See `verus-syntax` for attribute-based syntax
reference. Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a working example.

## Core Approach

1. **One function at a time.** Resolve `admit()` function by function,
   following the order from the `verification-order` skill if a
   verification plan exists. Do not move to the next function until the
   current one verifies cleanly.
   
   The current module's functions must NOT have `external_body`.
   Dependency functions in other modules may have `external_body` with
   specs; these are removed when that module is verified later.

2. **Keep trying.** When verification fails, read the error log carefully,
   try a different proof strategy, and iterate. You are capable of solving
   this — if one approach fails, try the next. Do not give up or ask for
   suggestions; work through possible approaches systematically.

3. **Never weaken specs.** If a spec is hard to prove, the proof strategy
   is wrong — not the spec. Do not relax `requires`, weaken `ensures`,
   or remove clauses to make proofs easier. The spec is the contract.

4. **Report genuine bugs.** If after thorough attempts you determine the
   failure is caused by a code bug (not a proof gap), report it immediately
   using the `bug-reporting` skill. Do not silently work around code bugs.

5. **Clean verification.** After all proofs pass, check for warnings and
   resolve them. A clean verification has zero errors AND zero warnings.
   Trigger warnings are especially common and must not be left: add
   explicit `#[trigger]` annotations or restructure quantifiers until
   all trigger warnings are gone.

## Verification Tool

Use `make verify-<crate> MODULE=<module>` to verify the current module during
proving. After all modules are done, run `make verify-<crate>` (no MODULE) to
confirm the full crate still passes. The output includes:
- **Verification result** — pass/fail with error details
- **Cheating detection** — flags `admit`, `assume`, `external_body`, `trusted`,
  cfg-gated exec code; all must be resolved in current module.
  `external_body` on direct callees in dependency modules is expected
  until those modules are verified; do not add `external_body` to
  functions the current module does not call. **Never** mark callers
  (upstream modules) as `external_body`
- **Coverage** — which functions have contracts

After verification passes, use the `ast-consistency` skill to check that
exec code was not accidentally modified during proving. Fix all
inconsistencies before finalizing.

---

## Workarounds

For unsupported syntax, external crate calls without specs, and unsupported
parameter types, follow the `verus-constraints` skill's escalation ladder.

## Proof Organization

- **Write proof helpers in `.proof.rs` from the start.** If a proof block
  would exceed ~5 lines, don't write it inline — define a `proof fn` in the
  `.proof.rs` file and call it from the inline `proof { }` block. Same for
  loop invariants with more than ~5 clauses: define a `spec fn` predicate in
  `.proof.rs` and reference it in the `invariant` clause. This avoids
  cluttering exec code and eliminates extraction work later.
- Keep proof fn granular: one lemma per function, chain via `assert ... by { lemma_call(); }`
- Default: make specs `opaque`, only `reveal()` where needed

# Verus Attribute-Based Syntax — Quick Reference

Use `#[verus_spec]` for exec functions, `verus! {}` for spec/proof functions.

Files in this directory:
- **SKILL.md** — this file, daily-use quick reference
- **GUIDE.md** — advanced patterns (ghost/tracked passing, dual_spec, closures, traits)

|---|---|

| Mark external_body | `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` |
| Loop invariants | `#[verus_spec(invariant ...)]` on loop |
| Proof blocks inside exec | `proof! { ... }` |
| Function-scoped ghost vars | `proof_decl! { ... }` |
| Spec fn / proof fn | `verus! { ... }` (unchanged) |

For advanced patterns (ghost/tracked passing, dual_spec, closures, traits),
see `GUIDE.md` in this skill directory.

## #[verus_spec] — Function Specifications

```rust
#[verus_spec(sum =>
    requires
        x < 100,
        y < 100,
    ensures
        sum < 200,
)]
fn my_exec_fun(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 {
    x + y
}
```

Named return (`sum =>`) binds the return value. Omit if not needed:

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    requires x < 100,
)]
fn do_something(x: u32) { /* ... */ }
```

Bare `#[verus_spec]` marks for verification with no specs:

```rust
#[verus_spec]
fn simple_function() { /* verified, no contracts */ }
```

Supported clauses: `requires`, `ensures`, `decreases`, `returns`, `with`.

## #[verus_verify] — Verification Hints

```rust
#[verus_verify]                    // mark for verification
#[verus_verify(external_body)]     // skip body verification
#[verus_verify(external)]          // skip entirely
#[verus_verify(rlimit(50))]        // resource limit
```

Combine with `#[verus_spec]`:

```rust
#[verus_verify(external_body)]
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x > 0,
    ensures ret == x,
)]
fn wrapper(x: u32) -> u32 { x }
```

## Loop Invariants

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    invariant
        v@ =~= Seq::new(i as nat, |k| k as u32),
)]
for i in 0..n {
    v.push(i);
}
```

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    invariant i <= 10,
)]
while i < 10 {
    i = i + 1;
}
```

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    invariant i <= 10,
    invariant_except_break i <= 9,
    ensures i == 10, ret == 10,
)]
loop {
    i = i + 1;
    if i == 10 { ret = i; break; }
}
```

## proof! { } — Proof Blocks

Block-scoped proof code inside exec functions:

```rust
#[verus_spec(requires x < 100, y < 100)]
fn test(x: u32, y: u32) {
    proof! {
        let u = my_spec_fun(x as int, y as int);
        my_proof_fun(u / 2, y as int);
        assert(f1(3) > 3) by { reveal(f1); };
        assert(x ^ x == 0u32) by (bit_vector);
    }
}
```

## proof_decl! { } — Function-Scoped Ghost Variables

Variables persist across the entire function (not just one block):

```rust
#[verus_spec]
fn test() {
    proof_decl! {
        let ghost mut x;
        let tracked y = false;
        x = 2int;
    }
    some_exec_call();
    proof! {
        assert(x == 2);  // still in scope
        assert(!y);
    }
}
```

Only `ghost` and `tracked` declarations allowed — no exec `let`, no exec calls.

## Spec/Proof Functions (verus! { })

```rust
verus! {

pub open spec fn is_valid(x: int) -> bool {
    x >= 0 && x < 100
}

proof fn lemma_validity(x: int)
    requires is_valid(x),
    ensures x + 1 < 101,
{}

} // verus!
```

description: "Determine function-level verification order within a module using the verification plan. Use at the start of proving to know which function to verify first and how to sequence work."

# Verification Order

## Purpose

When proving a module, you must verify functions in **dependency order**:
verify callees before callers. This avoids wasting effort on callers whose
callees don't yet have specs, and ensures each function's dependencies are
already proven when you reach it.

## How to Get the Order

A pre-generated verification plan may exist at:

```
{logs_dir}/verification-plan.json
```

If this file exists, use `show_fn_order.py` to display the function order:

```bash
# Show function order for a specific module
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "kernel::mm::phys::kpool"

# Glob pattern to match multiple modules
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "bitmap::*"
```

If the file does not exist, skip this step and use your best judgment for
function ordering (generally: leaf helpers first, public API functions last).

## How to Use the Order

1. **At the start of proving**, check for the plan and run `show_fn_order.py`.
2. **Verify functions in the listed order** (top to bottom = leaves first).
   The first function has no intra-module dependencies; later functions
   may call earlier ones.
3. **Do not skip ahead.** Resolve each function's `admit()` before moving
   to the next. This mirrors the proving-guide's "one function at a time"
   rule but with a concrete ordering.
4. **Cross-module deps** listed in the output tell you which dependency
   modules need specs. If a callee in another module lacks a spec, write
   an `assume_specification` or verify that module first.

## Output Format

```
## kernel::mm::phys::kpool
   crate: kernel  |  file: src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kpool.rs

    #  Function                        Line  In-module deps
  ───  ──────────────────────────────  ─────  ──────────────────────────────
    1  KpoolInner::alloc               L56   —
    2  KernelFrame::deref_mut          L160  —
    3  KernelFrame::clear              L144  KernelFrame::deref_mut
    4  Kpool::alloc                    L205  KpoolInner::alloc, clear
```

Use `-v` to also see cross-module dependency modules.

Functions are ordered so that by the time you reach function N, all its
intra-module dependencies (functions 1..N-1) are already verified.

I need to prove the Verus specs for `kpool.rs` which implements a kernel frame pool backed by a Bitmap. The module has 4 functions with contracts that need proofs: `Inner::new`, `Inner::alloc`, `Inner::alloc_range`, `Inner::free`.

## Current State
- kpool.spec.rs defines `inv()` as `self@.wf() && self.internal_inv()`
- kpool.proof.rs defines `View for Inner` (mapping to KpoolView) and `internal_inv()` as `true`
- KpoolView has fields: `start: int, num_pages: int, used_page_indices: Set<int>`
- KpoolView::wf() requires num_pages > 0, start % page_size == 0, all used indices in [0, num_pages)
- The `error!` macro calls cause Verus compilation failures (need cfg-gating)

## Dependencies with specs already:
- `Bitmap::alloc()` - full spec (alloc a bit, returns index, updates set_bits)
- `Bitmap::alloc_range(size)` - full spec (alloc range, returns start, updates set_bits)
- `Bitmap::clear(index)` - full spec (clear a bit, updates set_bits)
- `Bitmap::number_of_bits()` - ensures result == self@.num_bits, result > 0
- `usize::checked_mul` - vstd spec (None if overflow, Some otherwise)
- `Vec::is_empty` - vstd spec

## Dependencies WITHOUT specs:
- `FrameAddress::new(PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>) -> Self` — trivial constructor
- `FrameAddress::into_raw_value(self) -> usize` — returns underlying value
- `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>::into_raw_value(self) -> usize` — returns underlying value
- `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>::from_address(addr) -> Result<Self, Error>` — validates alignment
- `PhysicalAddress::from_raw_value(value: usize) -> Result<Self, Error>` — validates physical address
- `is_valid_physical_region(base: usize, size: usize) -> bool` — platform validation

## My Plan

### Step 1: cfg-gate error!/info!/trace! macros in kpool.rs
Add `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` before each logging macro in the verified impl block.

### Step 2: Add external_body specs to dependency functions
Add `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` + `#[verus_spec]` to:
- `FrameAddress::new`: ensures ret@ == address@, address.inv() ==> ret.inv()
- `FrameAddress::into_raw_value`: ensures ret as int == self@
- `PageAligned::into_raw_value` (Address trait impl): ensures ret as int == self@
- `PageAligned::from_address`: ensures Ok(pa) ==> pa@ == addr@ && pa.inv(); addr@ % page_size == 0 ==> result is Ok
- `PhysicalAddress::from_raw_value`: ensures Ok(a) ==> a@ == value as int; spec_phys_addr_valid(value as int) ==> result is Ok
- `is_valid_physical_region`: ensures result ==> base + size <= usize::MAX + 1, and forall i < size/page_size: spec_phys_addr_valid(base + i * page_size)
- Also strengthen PAGE_SIZE spec to add `result > 0`

### Step 3: Define spec_phys_addr_valid and strengthen internal_inv
In kpool.proof.rs:
```rust
pub uninterp spec fn spec_phys_addr_valid(addr: int) -> bool;

pub closed spec fn internal_inv(&self) -> bool {
    &&& self.base.inv()
    &&& self.bitmap.inv()
    &&& spec_page_size() > 0  
    &&& self.base@ + self.bitmap@.num_bits * spec_page_size() <= usize::MAX as int + 1
    &&& forall|i: int| 0 <= i < self.bitmap@.num_bits ==> spec_phys_addr_valid(self.base@ + i * spec_page_size())
}
```

### Step 4: Write proofs (in order: new, alloc, free, alloc_range)

**Inner::new**: After checked_mul succeeds and is_valid_physical_region returns true, establish all internal_inv conditions. The ensures about used_page_indices needs showing `bitmap@.set_bits =~= Set::new(|i| bitmap@.is_bit_set(i))`.

**Inner::alloc**: After bitmap.alloc() returns Ok(index):
- addr = base@ + index * PAGE_SIZE (page-aligned, valid phys)
- PhysicalAddress::from_raw_value(addr) succeeds (spec_phys_addr_valid)
- PageAligned::from_address succeeds (page-aligned)
- FrameAddress::new gives correct view
- page_index = index
After bitmap.alloc() returns Err: bitmap is_full => all pages used

**Inner::free**: 
- Compute index from addr subtraction/division
- bitmap.clear(index) maps directly to spec
- Need to show runtime usize division matches spec int division

**Inner::alloc_range**: Similar to alloc but with a for loop needing invariants.

## Specific Concerns

1. **Is spec_phys_addr_valid the right approach?** I need to connect is_valid_physical_region with PhysicalAddress::from_raw_value. An uninterpreted function seems like the cleanest way.

2. **In Inner::alloc, can PhysicalAddress::from_raw_value or PageAligned::from_address fail?** The spec says Err implies all pages used. If these fail after bitmap.alloc succeeds, the bitmap is modified but we return Err, violating self@ == old(self)@. So I need to prove they always succeed in this context.

3. **In Inner::free, the usize subtraction `addr.into_raw_value() - self.base.into_raw_value()` could wrap.** If addr@ < self.base@, it wraps, giving a large index. bitmap.clear will reject it. But I need to prove the spec's Err case still holds.

4. **Inner::alloc_range has a for loop** that constructs FrameAddresses. I'll need loop invariants that track the relationship between loop index, addresses, and the Vec state.

5. **Should spec_page_size() > 0 be in internal_inv?** It's a global property. Maybe better as a separate proof fact.

Please review this plan and point out any blind spots, issues, or improvements.

# Verus Verification Review Methodology

Review verification code with the same rigor as the verification itself. A
rubber-stamp review is worse than no review — it gives false confidence.

## Core Principles

- **Implementation is ground truth.** Check every spec against actual code
  behavior, not against what you think the code should do.
- **Stay independent and skeptical.** Do not trust claims at face value —
  not fix reports, not "it's a Verus limitation", not "the spec has to be
  that way". Verify everything yourself: read the code, run the commands,
  search vstd, reproduce the claimed limitation. Form your own judgment.
- **Be specific and actionable.** Every issue must point to a specific
  location and describe a specific fix. "Specs could be stronger" is not
  actionable. "`insert` is missing ensures for error code when table is full" is.

## Review Focus

### Primary: Spec Quality (reviewer's unique value)

If verification passes, the proof is correct — don't review proof technique.
Focus on whether specs are **meaningful and complete**. Refer to `spec-design`
skill for what good specs look like.

The reviewer's core mental model: **read each ensures clause as a caller who
has never seen the implementation.** Is every clause natural, directly usable,
and free of implementation assumptions? If you find yourself needing to look
at the code to understand why a clause is phrased that way, the spec is
probably mirroring the implementation.

- **Requires**: are preconditions necessary? Would the function work without
  them? Unnecessary requires narrow the usable interface.
- **Ensures**: are postconditions strong enough? Do they capture what callers
  actually need? `Err(_) => true` is useless.
- **Loop invariants**: do they capture the full state at each iteration, or
  do they only state what the prover needs to terminate?
- **Completeness**: are error paths specified? Is state preservation on error
  proven? Are there bidirectional failure conditions ("fails IFF X")?
- **Liveness**: under what conditions does the operation succeed?
  (`can_do_X() ==> result is Ok`)
- **Abstraction**: does the View type hide implementation details? Could the
  implementation be replaced without changing the View?

When reviewing a proposed fix, apply the same caller mental model: did the
fix express the missing property at the right abstraction level, or did it
patch the existing spec using implementation knowledge?

### Automated Checks (verify, don't review)

These should be confirmed but don't require judgment. See `proving-guide`
for verification tools and `ast-consistency` for exec fidelity tools.
- **Verification passes**: `make verify` reports 0 errors
- **Guardrails compliance**: no admit, assume, external_body, trusted,
  cfg-gated exec code, unjustified `uninterp spec fn` (use `detect_cheating`
  tool or `verus-constraints` rules)
- **Compilation**: `cargo build` succeeds without Verus features
- **Exec fidelity**: `ast-consistency` tools show no unintended changes

If you spot potential bugs during review, refer to `bug-reporting` skill for
classification and reporting format.

## Adversarial Dialogue (post-review)

When the pipeline enters dialogue mode after bulk fixes fail, the reviewer
drives a focused, turn-by-turn conversation with the fixer. Each turn
targets one specific issue (or a tightly-coupled bundle sharing one root cause).

### Skeptical Verifier Mindset

- **Don't trust claims.** If the fixer says "this is a Verus limitation" or
  "this can't be expressed", verify it yourself. Run the tool, read the error,
  search for counterexamples.
- **Search for precedent.** Before accepting a limitation claim, search known
  Verus projects (`verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`,
  ironfleet, page-table examples) for similar patterns that work.
- **Ask "why".** Demand specific evidence: error messages, minimal
  reproduction, links to Verus issues. "It doesn't work" is not evidence.
- **Don't be lazy.** Always use tools — run `make verify`, read files, search
  code. Never accept or reject a claim without checking it yourself.
- **Know when to stop.** A genuine limitation has: (a) a specific Verus error
  message, (b) no known workaround in verus-lang examples, (c) a clear
  explanation of why the pattern is unsupported. Mark such items BLOCKED
  with the evidence attached.

### Dialogue Protocol

Each reviewer turn writes a focused request file. To end the dialogue,
create the designated STOP file with content `RESOLVED` or `BLOCKED`.
Do not create the STOP file while issues remain unaddressed.

Here are the main blind spots I see.

## Blocking Issues

1. **`alloc_range` spec does not match the current implementation’s first error path**
   - **Impact:** Unprovable contract / wrong spec.
   - **Where:** `kpool.rs:173-209` vs `kpool.rs:211-216`
   - **Problem:** The code returns `Err` when `addrs` is non-empty, but the spec’s `Err(_)` case only allows `count == 0` or “no free range exists”.
   - **Fix:** Either:
     - add `requires old(addrs)@.len() == 0`, or
     - extend the `Err` postcondition to include `!old(addrs)@.is_empty()`.

2. **Step 1/2 rely on trusted shortcuts that the review guardrails explicitly reject**
   - **Impact:** Even if verification passes, the result is not review-clean.
   - **Where:** your proposed `cfg`-gating of logging macros; proposed `external_body` specs for address constructors/converters.
   - **Problem:** The review rules call out **no cfg-gated exec code**, **no unjustified `external_body`**, and **no unjustified uninterpreted specs**. Your plan introduces all three.
   - **Fix:** Minimize the trusted boundary:
     - do **not** cfg-gate exec statements inside verified code;
     - do **not** mark trivial wrappers like `FrameAddress::new` / `into_raw_value` external unless absolutely necessary;
     - put the trust boundary at the **platform validation layer** only, not every wrapper above it.

3. **The “conversion can’t fail after bitmap mutation” obligation is bigger than your plan states**
   - **Impact:** Violates `Err(_) => self@ == old(self)@`; for `alloc_range`, also violates `addrs@ == old(addrs)@`.
   - **Where:** `kpool.rs:145-155`, `kpool.rs:218-233`
   - **Problem:** You noticed this for `alloc`, but `alloc_range` is the sharper case: once `bitmap.alloc_range()` succeeds, any later `?` inside the loop would leave mutated pool state and possibly partially filled `addrs`.
   - **Fix:** Before proving `alloc`/`alloc_range`, prove a lemma of the form:
     - successful bitmap allocation + `old(self).inv()` ⇒ every generated address is valid and page-aligned.
     - If you can’t prove that, the code must be reordered.

## Non-Blocking Issues

4. **`spec_page_size() > 0` should not live only in `internal_inv`**
   - **Impact:** You still have `% spec_page_size()` and `/ spec_page_size()` in specs before `internal_inv` helps.
   - **Where:** `kpool.spec.rs:4-8`, `mod.spec.rs:32-44`, `frame.rs:34-39`
   - **Problem:** `wf()` already uses `spec_page_size()`. If positivity is only in `internal_inv`, that’s too late.
   - **Fix:** Strengthen the global `PAGE_SIZE` spec once.

5. **`free` needs a real wraparound lemma, not just “bitmap.clear will reject it”**
   - **Impact:** Risk of a proof gap in the success/error correspondence.
   - **Where:** `kpool.rs:257-280`
   - **Problem:** Spec uses mathematical subtraction; exec uses wrapped `usize` subtraction. You need to show wrapped underflow cannot produce an in-range index that makes `clear()` succeed.
   - **Fix:** Plan a dedicated arithmetic lemma using:
     - page alignment,
     - pool-size bound,
     - and the machine-width bound.

## Suggestions

6. **Be careful with `spec_phys_addr_valid`**
   - It can be the right abstraction, but only if it is the **single** trusted bridge between:
     - `is_valid_physical_region`, and
     - `PhysicalAddress::from_raw_value`.
   - Don’t also trust all the wrapper functions above it; that just inflates the TCB.

7. **`Inner::new`’s error spec is weak**
   - Not proof-blocking, but callers learn nothing on `Err`.
   - If you touch the contract anyway, consider specifying at least state preservation / failure cause shape.

Biggest takeaway: **fix the `alloc_range` contract mismatch first**, then **shrink the trusted boundary**. Those are the two issues most likely to derail the proof effort.
